module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Legendre's conjecture

*References:*
- [Landau Problems Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Twin_prime_conjecture)
- [Legendre Conjecture Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture)
- [Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter
namespace LegendreConjecture

/--
Does there always exist at least one prime between consecutive perfect squares?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem legendre_conjecture :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p := by
  sorry

/--
If there exists a constant `c > 0` such that
`(n + 1).nth Nat.Prime - n.nth Nat.Prime < (n.nth Nat.Prime) ^ (1 / 2 - c)` for all large `n`,
then Legendre's conjecture is asymptotically true.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at "https://github.com/mzhorvath1/formal-conjectures/blob/a4568d467b4f42884b6a4bd09c40d65f92113ee7/FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/LegendreConjecture.lean#L48"]
theorem bounded_gap_legendre
    (H : ∃ c > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (n + 1).nth Nat.Prime - n.nth Nat.Prime <
      (n.nth Nat.Prime : ℝ) ^ (1 / (2 : ℝ) - c)) :
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p := by
  sorry

/--
Ferreira proved that the conjecture is true for sufficiently large n.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem legendre_conjecture.ferreira_large_n :
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p := by
  sorry

end LegendreConjecture

findings.description: The module docstring's first reference, "Landau Problems Wikipedia Page", links to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Twin_prime_conjecture. That anchor is the Twin prime conjecture section, not Legendre's conjecture. The same link appears verbatim in TwinPrimes.lean and GoldbachConjecture.lean, so it looks like a copy-paste slip. The mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: The Landau's problems article has a dedicated section "===Legendre's conjecture===" (item 3: "Legendre's conjecture: Does there always exist at least one prime between consecutive perfect squares?"). The Twin prime conjecture section is a different section. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Landau%27s_problems&action=raw

status_issues.recorded: @[category research solved], with the docstring "Ferreira proved that the conjecture is true for sufficiently large n."
status_issues.source_status: Open. No accepted proof exists that Legendre's conjecture holds for all sufficiently large n. The only claimed proof is L. A. Ferreira's arXiv preprint 2307.08725. v1 (July 2023) and v4 (May 2026) are both marked "submitted to Annals of Mathematics"; OpenAlex lists it as an unpublished preprint with 0 citations. The preprint claims π(x+x^λ)−π(x) ~ x^λ/log x for every λ∈(0,1). That is beyond what the Riemann hypothesis is known to give; the paper itself says RH yields only λ > 1/2. No expert acceptance is recorded anywhere.
status_issues.evidence:
Wikipedia, Legendre's conjecture: {{unsolved|...}}, and "If Cramér's conjecture is true, Legendre's conjecture would follow for all sufficiently large n". This treats the large-n form as conditional. Ferreira is not mentioned under 'Partial results'.

Wikipedia, Prime gap: "The Lindelöf hypothesis ... would not be enough to imply that there is a prime number between n^2 and (n+1)^2 for n sufficiently large (see Legendre's conjecture). To verify this, a stronger result such as Cramér's conjecture would be needed." It gives the best unconditional exponent as θ = 0.525 (Baker–Harman–Pintz), short of the 1/2 needed.

Wikipedia, Landau's problems: "As of 2026, all four problems are unresolved."

The preprint's decisive step (Step 10, v4 source around line 513) goes from uniform convergence of ∫_C Υ(s,z)dz on compact subsets of the closed half-plane Re(s) ≥ 0 to analyticity "in an open neighborhood of the half-plane Re(s) ≥ 0". That does not follow: for Re(s) < 0 the integrand grows like exp(|t|(|arg s| − π/2)), so the argument does not give the continuation that Newman's Tauberian theorem needs. The paper's own 'Legendre's conjecture' is also the stronger 'at least two primes' form.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to @[category research open]. Reword the docstring to say that Ferreira claims this in an unrefereed preprint, or drop the attribution. The Lean statement itself (Legendre for all large n) can stay as it is.

review.notes:
No misformalizations found; the main theorem and both variants state what their docstrings and sources say.

1. `legendre_conjecture` (`answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n^2) ((n+1)^2), p.Prime`, with `n : ℕ`) is faithful to Wikipedia ("for every positive integer n") and to the Landau question. The polarity is right, and `research open` is correct. In Lean I checked two things:
   - `n = 0` has no witness, so the `n ≥ 1` hypothesis is needed.
   - Open and closed intervals give the same statement for every `n`, because squares are never prime.

2. `bounded_gap_legendre` is correct and not vacuous. The hypothesis is an open but believed-true statement that follows from Cramér's conjecture, and the `∃ c` makes large `c` harmless.
   - I wrote an independent ~35-line proof of its exact type, using `Nat.count`, `Nat.nth_lt_of_lt_count`, `Nat.le_nth_count` and `Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le`.
   - `example : type_of% @LegendreConjecture.bounded_gap_legendre := bgl_check` type-checks, and `#print axioms` shows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. So `research solved` is consistent.
   - I did not open the `formal_proof` link, since it points into a fork of formal-conjectures (github.com/mzhorvath1/...). The kind `formal_conjectures` means "proved in this repository", but at this commit the declaration is `sorry` here; `lean4` may be the more accurate kind. The implication is elementary, so `textbook` would arguably fit better than `research solved`. Neither point affects the mathematics.

3. `ferreira_large_n` states the standard one-prime Legendre conjecture for large n. Ferreira's paper calls the stronger "at least two primes" form "Legendre's conjecture". The Lean states the weaker, standard form, consistent with its docstring, so I did not treat this as a defect. The only problem is its status, reported above.

4. Outside this file: the sibling files `Andrica.lean`, `BrocardConjecture.lean` and `Oppermann.lean` also carry `ferreira_large_*` declarations tagged `research solved` on the same unaccepted preprint. They likely have the same status issue.
